newsitem.title: CANADA: No quick investigation on Canada wheat, Daley says.
newsitem.headline: No quick investigation on Canada wheat, Daley says.

text.p: U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley raised the sensitive issue of Canadian wheat exports with Canadian Trade Minister Sergio Marchi on Tuesday.
But he said in an interview that Washington was unlikely to move quickly to an investigation of whether Canada was dumping wheat.

Lawmakers from North Dakota and other northern states have voiced concern about Canadian wheat exports, which are not limited by any agreement, but which the legislators assert have unfairly pushed down prices and lowered the income of their wheat farmers.

"I've requested that he understand the degree of concern by the North Dakota farmers and the importance of this issue to the political representatives of those states," Daley said after his meeting with Marchi.

U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said on Thursday that the Commerce Department would meet soon with U.S. wheat producers to determine whether an investigation into dumping -- selling grain at an unfairly cheap price -- was warranted.
Canadian Agriculture Minister Lyle Vanclief responded that three investigations have demonstrated that such complaints were unfounded and that Canada was trading fairly.
Asked to react, Daley said: "I don't know if there has ever been an investigation and a determination that anything's unfounded."

He said meetings with representatives of the wheat industry and Congressional staffs would be useful in gathering the kind of information that was required to decide whether to proceed with an investigation, which he recognized would be a serious step.
"There would have to be a lot more information gathered before a determination would be even made to do that," he said.

Ironically, Canada and the United States have generally found themselves on the same side in international trade negotiations pushing for lower farm trade barriers and subsidies, even though they differ on specific issues.
The next round of negotiations under the World Trade Organization is to begin in 1999. Daley said he would like an agreement that year.
"Our goal is not to have these drag on," he said.
